Resettlement · ESIA and RAP

A dated register of structures, at the cut-off date

In lender-financed projects, the cut-off date marks the start of the census; assets put in place after it are not compensated. From dated imagery we build a register of the structures inside the project’s emprise on that date, each with an ID, coordinates and the image date, then the changes up to the census. It supports the census and the asset inventory; it does not replace them.

Request a proposal The legal framework

The cut-off date

What existed, and on what date

A resettlement plan published in January 2025 for a World Bank-financed road project in the DRC defines the cut-off date as follows: “C’est la date qui marque le début de l’opération de recensement des personnes et de leurs biens. […] les biens (maisons, champs, arbres…) mis en place après la date limite ne sont pas indemnisés” (resettlement plan, 2025). It is the date that marks the start of the census of people and their assets, and assets such as houses, fields and trees put in place after it are not compensated.

On that project the cut-off date was set three times, at 13 November 2021, 6 March 2023 and then 15 August 2024, and the emprise moved from 9 m to 15 m on the first 10 km, with the remaining 140 km to be updated at 15 m, or 12 m in constrained areas. For another World Bank-financed project, a plan set the cut-off date at 2 July 2021, the first day of a census held from 2 to 22 July 2021, under the World Bank’s Environmental and Social Standard 5 (resettlement plan).

When the emprise or the timetable changes, the cut-off date can be redefined: a dated image survey shows what existed at each date.

No link with AfriScan

The projects mentioned are public programmes, cited from their published documents. They imply no relationship with AfriScan.

The framework

Congolese law and lenders’ standards

Checked on 27 September 2026. A summary of the public rules for orientation; it is not legal advice. Lenders’ standards apply on top of Congolese law where the financing requires them.

Congolese law

  • Land tenure. “Le sol est la propriété exclusive, inaliénable et imprescriptible de l’Etat”: the land is the exclusive, inalienable and imprescriptible property of the State (Loi n° 73-021 of 20 July 1973, art. 53). According to the resettlement policy framework the World Bank published in 2013, the inquiry this law provides for includes a census of the people present on the land or carrying out an activity there, a description of the site and an inventory.
  • Expropriation. According to the same document, Loi n° 77-001 of 22 February 1977 counts among expropriable rights “les droits de jouissance des communautés locales sur les terres domaniales”, local communities’ rights of use over State land.
  • Mining. “En cas de déplacement des populations, l’opérateur minier est tenu préalablement de procéder à l’indemnisation, à la compensation et à la réinstallation des populations concernées”: where people are displaced, the mining operator must first compensate and resettle them (Mining Code, art. 281, since 2018).
  • Electricity. A servitude is preceded by a notification and a record of condition; a permanent emprise gives a right to compensation, including for “les occupants des terres rurales qui ont effectivement mis le fonds en valeur”, occupants of rural land who have actually developed it (Loi n° 14/011, arts 111 to 113).
  • ESIA. The impact study includes “l’inventaire précis et détaillé de l’état initial du site, de son environnement naturel, socio-économique et humain”, a precise and detailed inventory of the site’s initial state and of its natural, socio-economic and human environment, and anyone may consult the reports (Décret n° 14/019, arts 19 and 38).

Lenders’ standards

Where a project is financed by IFC, by a bank that applies the Equator Principles or by the World Bank, IFC Performance Standard 5 or the World Bank’s Environmental and Social Standard 5 applies to resettlement. Both call for a census and an asset inventory closed at a cut-off date.

Our register supports the cut-off-date record: it establishes what the imagery showed at a known date. It replaces neither the census, nor the asset inventory, nor the consultation of affected people.

Who decides

Who is eligible, and for what, is decided in the RAP, with the affected people and the competent authorities. Our surveys support the census and the asset inventory; they do not replace them, and they record no one.

What you receive

A register at the cut-off date, then the changes

The cut-off-date register

Each structure found inside the project’s emprise, with an ID, its coordinates, its distance from the route or boundary and the image date, on imagery whose date is known.

Categories

Main building, outbuilding, enclosure or building under construction, from what the imagery shows, to prepare the inventory. Compensation needs verification on the ground.

Changes up to the census

Structures that appeared or disappeared between the cut-off date and the census, or between two cut-off dates, flagged automatically and confirmed by an analyst.

Estimated households

On request, an estimated number of households from the structures, with the assumptions stated, to prepare the consultation. It is not a census.

A sheet per grievance

For a point or a plot, the dated images that cover it, on one sheet, to show what stood there at each date.

A dated record

Imagery, register and maps brought together with a digital fingerprint of each file and an independent timestamp, to support legal and community processes.

Delivered as a PDF report and GeoPackage, GeoJSON, KMZ and Shapefile files that your teams and your consultants can load into their own maps. The same method, for every country: resettlement cut-off-date baselines · dated imagery and cut-off dates.

By sector

Where cut-off dates are prepared

Mining expansions

Mining Code art. 281 requires compensation and resettlement before anyone is displaced. The dated register prepares the census inside the expansion’s footprint.

Power lines

Before the servitude, the electricity law provides for a record of condition and, for a permanent emprise, compensation after a declaration of public utility.

Railways and roads

Frequently asked questions

Can the register stand in for the census?

No. It establishes what the imagery showed at a known date and supports the census and asset inventory. It does not replace them, it records no one, and it sets neither entitlements nor compensation.

Why does the imagery have to be dated?

Because a cut-off-date register must say what existed on that date. Online map basemaps carry no capture date, so we work from a satellite scene acquired for the project, a drone survey or dated imagery you already hold, and every report names its sources.

What if the cut-off date is redefined?

We build the register for each date chosen, where imagery exists for those dates, and show the structures that appeared or disappeared between them. If the emprise changes width, the register is measured again against the new emprise.

Do you give numbers of people or households?

We do not count people. On request, we estimate a number of households from the structures, with the assumptions stated in the report. It is an estimate to prepare the consultation and the census, not a census.

Are the categories enough for compensation?

No. The categories (main building, outbuilding, enclosure, building under construction) describe what the imagery shows; they establish neither use, nor ownership, nor value. Compensation needs verification on the ground.

Can you look into a grievance about a plot?

For a point or a grievance, we gather the dated images that cover it on one sheet, to show what stood there at each date. The sheet supports the review of the grievance; it does not decide it.

Prepare your cut-off date on dated facts

Send the project's emprise (Shapefile, GeoPackage, KML or GeoJSON), the planned or already fixed cut-off date and the census date. We reply with an imagery plan and a written proposal.
